title: Climbing Mera Peak: Full Guide
excerpt: Mera Peak, 6,476 m, is the highest trekking peak in Nepal. The full guide: the Hinku valley route, acclimatization, the glacier summit day, gear, permits and cost.
seoTitle: Climbing Mera Peak: Route, Gear, Permit and Cost

content.value: In the small hours of the night, at high camp at 5,900 m, climbers buckle on their crampons, tie into a rope and set out onto the wide glacier that leads to the summit of Mera, 6,476 m (21,247 ft). Mera Peak is the highest trekking peak in Nepal, rising above the Hinku valley in the east of the country, not far from Everest. Its normal route requires no complex technical climbing, but it does require good fitness, patient acclimatization and a summit day on a glacier with crampons, an ice axe and a rope. The climbing seasons are spring and fall, and with us it is a 19-day expedition.

For many people, Mera is the first summit above 6,000 m, the step between a high-altitude trek and real mountaineering. Here is what you need to know before you decide: what makes this mountain accessible and what makes it hard, how our route through the Hinku valley works day by day, how acclimatization works, what happens at high camp and on summit day, what gear is required and what the price includes.
A high summit, not technical, and not easy

Mera Peak lies in the heart of the Nepal Himalaya, south of Everest, above the Hinku valley. It is a quiet, wild valley that far fewer trekkers reach than the neighboring Khumbu valley, where the Everest Base Camp trek runs. Mera stands 6,476 m high, higher than any summit in the Alps or the Caucasus, and it is the highest of the peaks that Nepal calls trekking peaks.

The word "trekking" misleads. Mera is not a trek: above high camp the way crosses a glacier, with crevasses that are sometimes hidden under snow, so you move in crampons and with an ice axe, with the climbers roped together. What makes it accessible is that the normal route has no rock or ice walls that call for advanced climbing technique. We grade the climb as challenging.

The main difficulty, as on any high mountain, is altitude. At the summit every breath brings in roughly half the oxygen it would at sea level, and the cold on summit day is the cold of a mountain above 6,000 m. That is the difference between Mera and a trek: the same fitness for long walking days, and on top of it a glacier, a night in a tent and a long summit day that starts in the middle of the night.

content.title: ✦ Five peaks above 8,000 m
content.value: On a clear day the summit of Mera looks out on five of the six highest mountains in the world: Everest (8,848 m), Kangchenjunga, Lhotse, Makalu and Cho Oyu, alongside many more peaks above 7,000 m.
Our route, day by day
The HighAir Mera Peak expedition lasts 19 days, from arrival in Kathmandu to departure. The altitudes in brackets are those of the overnight stop or of the high point of that day:

items: Day 1: arrival in Kathmandu and transfer to the hotel.
Day 2: preparation day in Kathmandu and a gear check.
Day 3: flight to Lukla and a walk to Paiya (2,790 m).
Day 11: from Khare up to high camp (5,900 m), after technical training on the glacier.
Day 12: summit day (6,476 m) and down to Khare (5,045 m).
Day 13: spare day for bad weather at Khare (5,045 m).
Day 16: crossing the Zatrwa La pass (4,600 m) and down to Lukla (2,860 m).
Day 17: flight from Lukla to Kathmandu or Ramechhap.
Day 18: spare day in case of bad weather, or a free day in Kathmandu.
Day 19: transfer to the airport and flight home.

content.value: Two principles guide the itinerary. The first is a gradual approach. From Lukla there is a short way into the Hinku valley, over the Zatrwa La pass at 4,600 m, but it takes the body high too fast in the first days. So on the way in we take the long route, through Paiya, Pangkongma and Ningsow, and sleep four nights below 3,200 m before entering the Hinku valley. The pass is crossed only on the way back, when the body is already adapted to altitude.

The second principle is a safety margin: an acclimatization day in Thagnag before going above 5,000 m, a spare day at Khare for the summit, and a spare day at the end of the trip in case the weather delays the flight from Lukla.

content.title: ✦ In slowly, out quickly
content.value: On the way in it takes 8 days from Lukla to Khare, including an acclimatization day. On the way out you reach Lukla from Khare in 3 days, over the Zatrwa La pass. That difference is the acclimatization.
From Lukla to the Hinku valley
Forests, villages and rivers

For the first four nights after landing in Lukla you sleep below 3,200 m, and the trails climb and drop between small villages, forests and rivers. This is the green part of the journey, and it is very different from the glacial landscape waiting higher up. Throughout the trek you sleep in teahouses, the simple lodges of Nepal, in twin rooms, and three meals a day, chosen from the menu, are included in the price. Every climber has a personal porter who carries up to 25 kg, and you walk with a daypack.

content.caption: A river between boulders and trees, with a snowy peak at the head of the valley

content.value: Kothe, Thagnag and Khare

On the seventh day you reach Kothe, 3,700 m, in the Hinku valley itself, and from there continue up the valley to Thagnag, 4,350 m. Here comes the acclimatization day of the route: an extra night at the same altitude, which lets the body adapt before the jump above 5,000 m. On the tenth day you reach Khare, 5,045 m, the last teahouse stop before the mountain.
Acclimatization: altitude sets the pace

The main risk on Mera is not technical but physiological. The higher you go, the less oxygen each breath brings in, and the body needs time to adapt. The accepted rule in mountain medicine is that above 3,000 m you do not raise your sleeping altitude by more than 500 m a night, and you add an extra night of acclimatization for every 1,000 m of sleeping altitude gained. For some climbers even this pace is too fast, so listen to your body.

Altitude sickness usually starts with a headache, sometimes joined by loss of appetite, dizziness, fatigue and nausea. When symptoms get worse despite rest at the same altitude, you descend. With us the decision to continue always belongs to the guide, and safety comes before the summit. Every group carries a pulse oximeter and a Magnus satellite device.

Our itinerary is built around this principle: four low nights at the start, an acclimatization day in Thagnag before passing 5,000 m, and after the summit a descent on the same day to sleep in Khare, far lower than high camp. In the mountains there is no promise of reaching the summit, but there is always a commitment to safety above all.
High camp and summit day
A night in a tent

On day 11, after technical training on the glacier above Khare, you climb straight to high camp at 5,900 m. The night at high camp is spent in HighAir twin tents, and every other night of the trek is in a teahouse. From high camp the view of the great peaks of the region already opens up, and the night there is short: you go to sleep early, because the start for the summit is in the middle of the night. On day 13 a spare day waits at Khare, in case the weather means the summit day has to move.

content.caption: A HighAir tent on the snow, below a snowy mountain wall

content.value: Summit day on the glacier

Summit day starts in the small hours of the night, usually between 2 and 3 in the morning. You move by headlamp, roped together, at a slow and steady pace, on wide snow slopes that rise gradually. Sunrise catches the climbers on the way, and with it the view opens: Everest, Lhotse, Makalu, Cho Oyu and Kangchenjunga. The last section, below the summit dome, is short and steeper, and when the snow is frozen a rope is sometimes fixed there.

The summit is only halfway. In our itinerary you descend on the same day not just to high camp but all the way to Khare, 5,045 m, which makes it the longest and most demanding walking day of the trip. Going down to a lower altitude is also part of safety: the night after the summit you sleep about 850 m lower than the night before it.
Technical gear and training

On the Mera glacier you walk with crampons, an ice axe and a rope, and before summit day participants are trained on this equipment. On summit day every climber has a personal climbing guide. Personal gear, meaning clothing, footwear and climbing gear, is not included in the price, and a full gear list is sent to every registrant after registration. A climbing gear rental kit is available for 300 dollars.

The most important item is a pair of high-altitude mountain boots that fit crampons and keep your feet warm in the cold of summit day. After them come warm clothing in layers, warm gloves and sunglasses suited to snow. Before departure you receive a personal gear checklist and an online gear consultation, and the group meets the guide on an online preparation call, so you reach Nepal with the right gear, already knowing the people you will climb with.

content.value: The flight to Lukla

The expedition starts and ends in Lukla, 2,860 m, the village that is home to the airport of the Everest region. In our package the flights to Lukla and back are by plane, and they are included in the price. Lukla airport is considered one of the most challenging in the world because of its short runway, and flights stop whenever the weather does not allow them.

In the busy seasons most flights to Lukla leave from the airport at Manthali in Ramechhap district, a few hours' drive from Kathmandu, not from Kathmandu itself. In our itinerary the return flight from Lukla lands in Kathmandu or Ramechhap. If you prefer, you can fly Kathmandu–Lukla–Kathmandu by helicopter for an extra 800 dollars per person. Day 18 of the itinerary is a spare day in Kathmandu in case the flight from Lukla is delayed, and if it is not needed it becomes a free day in the city.
Permits, visa and insurance

Climbing Mera Peak requires a climbing permit, issued by the Nepal Mountaineering Association through a registered local agency, as well as entry permits for the area. The permit price depends on the season, and it is lower in the fall than in spring. The climbing permit and the entry permits are included in the price of our expedition.

Most visitors, including UK, EU, US, Canadian and Australian citizens, get a Nepal tourist visa on arrival at Kathmandu airport or apply online in advance. For a 19-day trip you need the 30-day visa, which costs 50 US dollars (as of 2026) and is not included. Travel and medical insurance is not included either. Before buying a policy, check that it covers climbing up to 6,476 m, including rescue and helicopter evacuation.
When to go

Nepal has two main climbing seasons: spring, before the monsoon, and fall, after it. Our Mera expeditions depart in April and May, and in September and October. In the fall, after the rains end, the air is usually clearer and the views open, but the nights at altitude are cold. In spring the days are warmer in the lower part of the route, and clouds sometimes build up in the afternoon.

In the monsoon season, in the summer months, rain and cloud stop flights to Lukla and turn the forest trails to mud, and in winter the cold at altitude is very harsh. That is why the good windows are the ones before and after the monsoon.
Who it suits

Mera suits anyone who wants to stand above 6,000 m for the first time without moving on to technical climbing. Previous climbing experience is not a requirement: if you can walk about 20 km a day, enjoy a challenge and come with strong motivation, the climb can suit you. Previous high-altitude trekking experience, ideally above 4,500 m, is recommended, because it teaches you how your body reacts to altitude and to long days.

A medical certificate and a health declaration are conditions for departure, and anyone who does not meet the health or physical requirements will not be able to join. The best preparation is long uphill hikes with a pack on your back in the months before departure. Anyone who prefers to stay on the trail, with no glacier and no rope, will find the same region and the same views on the Everest Base Camp trek, up to 5,545 m, and we have written a complete guide to it.

content.value: Good to know: the climb is led by experienced local Sherpa guides who speak English and have long experience leading groups in the mountains. Basic English, enough to follow instructions on the trail, is worth having. Following the instructions of the crew is mandatory, and the route may change according to the weather and the judgment of the guides.
What it costs and what is included

The Mera Peak expedition costs 3,800 US dollars per person. It includes transfers between the airport and the hotel in Kathmandu, dinners at a restaurant before and after the climb, 3 nights in a 4-star hotel in Kathmandu in a single room with breakfast, domestic flights to Lukla and back, teahouse accommodation in shared rooms along the trek and HighAir twin tents at high camp, full service at high camp with cooking gear and food for the altitude, all entry permits for the trek and the Mera Peak climbing permit, three meals a day from the menu, 2 liters of hot water a day, a shower and attached toilet where available on the route, a personal climbing guide for every climber on summit day, professional local English-speaking guides, a personal porter for every participant, up to 25 kg per person, a first aid kit carried by the guides, a pulse oximeter for the group and a satellite device, a personal area in the HighAir app, a personal gear checklist with an online gear consultation, an online preparation call with your group and guide, and a gift kit with a cap, a dry-fit shirt and a 100-liter duffel bag.

Not included: international flights, travel and medical insurance, lunch and dinner at the hotel in Kathmandu, personal gear and climbing gear (a rental kit costs 300 dollars), tips for guides and porters (250 dollars per person), a summit bonus for the guides (250 dollars per person), the Nepal visa (50 dollars), vaccinations and travel clinic advice, and the extras the teahouses charge for separately, such as internet, laundry, alcohol and additional meals. A fourth hotel night in Kathmandu, if needed, is not included. At extra cost you can fly by helicopter from Kathmandu to Lukla and back (800 dollars per person) and upgrade to a single room in the teahouses (20 dollars a night).
Note that in the event of an early descent from the mountain, for any reason, the additional costs, such as extra hotel nights, meals and flight changes, are borne by the climber.
Mera Peak with HighAir

At HighAir we climb Mera Peak in spring and fall, in groups of up to 12 participants, and the success rate we publish on the mountain is 80 percent. Our itinerary is built around a gradual approach to the Hinku valley, an acclimatization day before 5,000 m and spare days for the summit and the flight.

content.value: A portion of the proceeds from every expedition we run is dedicated to supporting cancer patients, because the mountains, in our view, are also a way of giving back. Every climber you see on the summits of the world started once, on one mountain. If Mera is your first summit above 6,000 m, we are here.
Frequently asked questions
How many days does it take to climb Mera Peak?

The HighAir expedition lasts 19 days, from arrival in Kathmandu to departure. 14 of them are spent between landing in Lukla and getting back there, including an acclimatization day in Thagnag and summit day. There is also a preparation day in Kathmandu and a spare day in case of bad weather.
Do you need climbing experience to climb Mera Peak?

Previous climbing experience is not a requirement, and high-altitude trekking experience, ideally above 4,500 m, is recommended. The route requires no complex technical climbing, but on the glacier you walk with crampons, an ice axe and a rope, and before summit day participants are trained on the equipment. Good fitness, the ability to walk about 20 km a day and a medical certificate are required.
How much does it cost to climb Mera Peak?

The HighAir expedition costs 3,800 US dollars per person, and the price includes the flights to Lukla, accommodation, meals throughout the trek, the guides, the porters, the entry permits and the climbing permit. Not included are international flights, insurance, personal gear, the Nepal visa (50 dollars), tips (250 dollars) and a summit bonus for the guides (250 dollars).
When is the season for climbing Mera Peak?

Spring and fall, before and after the monsoon. Our expeditions depart in April and May, and in September and October. In the monsoon season, in the summer months, rain and cloud disrupt flights to Lukla and the trails.
Which permits do you need to climb Mera Peak?
A climbing permit issued by the Nepal Mountaineering Association, and entry permits for the area. The permit price depends on the season. Both are included in the price of our expedition.
What language do the guides speak?
The climb is led by experienced local Sherpa guides who speak English and have long experience leading groups in the mountains.
